headline: U.S. wholesale inflation hits 6.5%; Stellantis fight moves to its global CEO
briefing: U.S. wholesale prices rose 6.5% over the past year, the most since 2022, which pushed stocks lower Friday and keeps interest-rate increases in play on both sides of the border. Ottawa's dispute with Stellantis over the Brampton plant now moves to a meeting with the automaker's global chief executive, with a 30-day clock running before a threatened lawsuit. Microsoft says its email outage is easing, oil is holding just under US$96, and in Washington Sen. Chris Van Hollen is challenging Chuck Schumer to lead the new Democratic Senate majority.

keyDates.label: New municipal term; Israeli cabinet meets
keyDates.why: Ontario councils and the appointed regional chairs begin their four-year term, Israel's security cabinet meets after ordering readiness for a possible Iran strike, and the Southeast Asian summit Carney is attending opens in Manila.

keyDates.label: OSAP bill expected
keyDates.why: Ontario is expected to table its legislation on student aid at private career colleges when the legislature sits Monday.

keyDates.label: APEC summit; Alaska ranked-choice count
keyDates.why: Carney meets Xi in Shenzhen on Nov. 18–19, and Alaska tabulates its Peltola–Sullivan Senate race.

keyDates.label: Senate Democrats pick a leader
keyDates.why: Democratic senators vote by secret ballot between Chuck Schumer and challenger Chris Van Hollen for majority leader.

keyDates.label: Bank of Canada and Fed rate decisions
keyDates.why: Both central banks decide the same day; rising U.S. wholesale inflation and high oil prices keep further hikes on the table.

keyDates.label: Stellantis default deadline
keyDates.why: The 30 days Ottawa gave Stellantis on Nov. 12 to repay subsidies or reverse course run out, after which the government says it will sue.

stories.headline: Stellantis standoff heads to global CEO as Ford stays quiet on Brampton
stories.summary: Industry Minister Mélanie Joly says Stellantis owes Ottawa hundreds of millions of dollars and has 30 days to pay or be taken to court, after rejecting the automaker's offer to return $24 million. She says the next step is a meeting with the company's global chief executive, and Premier Doug Ford had little to say after Thursday's talks.
stories.now: Joly met Stellantis, Ontario government representatives and Unifor, the union for more than 9,000 of the company's Canadian workers, in Toronto on Thursday and said afterward she was fed up. A Stellantis executive said the company would return $24 million in federal support; Joly called that insufficient, said the true amount is in the hundreds of millions without giving a figure, and said Ottawa will sue if it is not repaid within the 30-day default period that began Thursday. CP24 reported Friday that Ford offered few words after the meeting and that Joly described a meeting with Stellantis's global chief executive as the next step; Unifor officials said Brampton workers feel let down. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has called on Prime Minister Carney to fire Joly; Carney, who has said he knew some aspects of the deal beforehand, has backed her and called the sale only a partial fix. No lawsuit has been filed, and the sale to armoured-vehicle maker Roshel is expected to close by the end of the year.
stories.backstory: The Brampton plant built Dodge and Chrysler cars and has been idle for about three years while workers stayed on paid layoff. In May 2022 Ottawa agreed to give Stellantis $529 million to retool its Brampton and Windsor plants, and the company had planned to build the Jeep Compass in Brampton. In October 2025 it moved that vehicle to Illinois as U.S. tariffs on Canadian-made cars took hold. Stellantis signed a memorandum of understanding with Roshel in September, Unifor's contract expired Sept. 20, and the union declared an impasse over the plant's future.

timeline.event: Ottawa pledges $529 million to retool Brampton and Windsor plants
Stellantis moves Jeep Compass production to Illinois

Carney calls the sale a betrayal

stories.why: The sale ends hopes that a major GTA auto plant would restart vehicle production, and it tests whether governments can enforce the conditions attached to public subsidies. It also shows how U.S. tariffs are pulling auto investment out of Ontario.
stories.impact: Thousands of Peel Region families depend on the plant and its parts suppliers, and most laid-off workers have no guarantee of a job with the new owner. Taxpayers have a stake too: the gap between the $24 million Stellantis has offered and the hundreds of millions Ottawa says it is owed may now be settled in court.

stories.headline: Oil heads for second weekly drop despite Hormuz tanker blasts; UN watchdog presses Iran
stories.summary: Brent crude traded just under US$96 a barrel on Friday and is still on course for a second straight weekly decline, even after President Trump said the United States no longer needs an agreement with Iran. Iran reported more tankers hit by mines near the Strait of Hormuz, and the United Nations nuclear agency urged Tehran to let inspectors back in.
stories.now: Brent settled up 3.3% at US$95.82 a barrel on Thursday and was near US$95.71 early Friday, which Investing.com said leaves it on track for a weekly decline of about 2.4% after a 16% plunge the week before. U.S. benchmark WTI (West Texas Intermediate) was around US$88.49 in early New York trading. Iran's Revolutionary Guards navy said a tanker carrying liquefied natural gas struck a mine and exploded east of the strait, and Iran's army said two more oil tankers caught fire after hitting mines, on top of four it reported Thursday; none of this has been independently confirmed, and the U.S. military says it has cleared the main routes. The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), the UN nuclear watchdog, called on Iran on Friday to reopen its nuclear sites to inspection; Tehran says that is not possible in the current security situation. Trump has told Vice-President JD Vance, who led the U.S. side of the talks, to turn to alleged fraud in Democratic-led states instead, while the U.S. naval blockade and sanctions stay in place. Israel's security cabinet, which reportedly ordered the army to step up preparations for a possible strike, is due to meet Sunday.
stories.backstory: The U.S. and Israel began striking Iran on Feb. 28, and Iran choked traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, route for about a fifth of the world's oil. A June peace memorandum briefly reopened it but collapsed in July, and the U.S. imposed a blockade on Iranian shipping. Qatar gave Iran a new draft deal on Oct. 25. Trump has said the war will end soon, one way or the other.

timeline.event: Qatar hands Iran a new draft deal
Brent peaks above US$117

Israeli cabinet reportedly orders strike readiness; Iran warns of wider retaliation
Trump says no deal with Iran is needed; Brent settles at US$95.82
Iran reports more tankers hitting mines; IAEA urges Iran to readmit inspectors

stories.why: Oil prices are the main driver of higher inflation in Canada and the U.S.; the October spike is why the Bank of Canada raised rates on Oct. 28.
stories.impact: Lower crude usually reaches GTA gas pumps within days, and this month's drop has eased fuel and delivery costs. With Trump stepping back from talks, tankers reportedly hitting mines and Israel raising readiness, that relief could reverse quickly.

stories.headline: U.S. wholesale inflation hits 6.5%, highest in nearly four years
stories.summary: Prices charged by U.S. producers rose 0.3% in October and 6.5% from a year earlier, the biggest annual increase since November 2022. The monthly figure was slightly below forecasts, but U.S. stocks turned lower Friday morning.
stories.now: The U.S. producer price index, which tracks what businesses receive for goods and services before they reach shoppers, rose 0.3% in October, a little under the 0.4% economists expected; the 6.5% annual rate compared with a 6.6% forecast. Leaving out food and energy, prices were up 0.3% on the month and 5% on the year. Wholesale energy prices slipped 0.1% after a sharp rise in September, with diesel down 7.9%, while wholesale food prices jumped 1.3%, the most since February. Stocks opened mixed and then fell: by late morning the S&P 500 was down roughly 0.8% to 1% and the Nasdaq about 1.6%, with Nvidia among the decliners, according to Yahoo Finance and CNBC. Some analysts quoted in U.S. coverage expect the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates at its December meeting.
stories.backstory: Wholesale prices often signal where consumer prices are heading a few months later. Oil surged after the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran began in February and disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, with Brent crude peaking above US$117 in late October, and tariffs have added to import costs. The Federal Reserve held its rate on Oct. 28, the same day the Bank of Canada raised its policy rate to 2.5%, its first increase in more than three years. Canada's annual inflation rate was 3.1% in September.

timeline.event: Iran war begins; oil prices start climbing
Canada's inflation rate edges up to 3.1%
Fed holds; Bank of Canada raises its rate to 2.5%
U.S. 10-year Treasury yield rises to about 5.09%
U.S. wholesale inflation reported at 6.5% for October

stories.why: Persistent price pressure in the United States makes further interest-rate increases there more likely. Canadian bond yields and mortgage rates tend to follow U.S. ones, and the Bank of Canada decides on the same day as the Fed, Dec. 9.
stories.impact: If you are renewing a mortgage or carrying a variable-rate loan in Ontario, higher U.S. rates raise the odds of higher borrowing costs here. Rising U.S. wholesale food prices can also feed into grocery bills, since Ontario imports much of its fresh produce from the U.S.

stories.headline: Microsoft says email is recovering; Unity Health reports service gradually returning
stories.summary: Microsoft's Outlook email outage, which began Thursday and disrupted Toronto hospitals, schools, City Hall and VIA Rail, eased on Friday as the company reported progress and backed-up mail started to clear. Unity Health Toronto, which declared a Code Grey on Thursday, says its email is gradually returning to normal; Microsoft has not confirmed a root cause.
stories.now: Unity Health Toronto, which runs St. Michael's, St. Joseph's and Providence, said in an update that email services are gradually returning to normal and that patient care was never affected. The University of Toronto, Seneca Polytechnic, George Brown Polytechnic, Toronto City Hall and VIA Rail also reported problems on Thursday. Reports put the peak at more than 130,000 user complaints, with organizations in more than 70 countries affected. Microsoft said servers unexpectedly became unavailable and that a process handling secure connections was overwhelmed, straining the rest of its systems; it says there is no sign of a cyberattack, warns that intermittent problems may continue, and has promised a report on the incident. A technology expert writing for The Conversation noted Friday that the company's account has shifted and that no root cause has been named.
stories.backstory: Many hospitals, universities, governments and businesses rent email and office software from Microsoft as an online service, known as Microsoft 365, rather than running their own servers. That means a single fault at the company can hit thousands of organizations at once. In July 2024 a faulty update from security firm CrowdStrike crashed Windows computers worldwide and disrupted GTA hospitals and airports. Ontario hospitals use Code Grey to signal the loss of essential infrastructure such as power, water or computer systems.

timeline.event: CrowdStrike update crashes Windows systems worldwide, hitting GTA hospitals
Outlook outage begins; Unity Health Toronto declares Code Grey
Microsoft says recovery is not working as expected
Microsoft reports recovery progress; Unity Health says email is returning

stories.why: The outage shows how much hospitals, schools and governments depend on one company's online services for basic communication. A long disruption slows everything from appointment notices to internal approvals.
stories.impact: If your workplace, school or hospital uses Outlook, some messages sent since Thursday may arrive late, so phone for anything urgent. Hospital care in Toronto has continued, and Microsoft says there is no indication of an attack.

stories.headline: Van Hollen challenges Schumer to lead the new Senate majority
stories.summary: Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen said Thursday night he will run against Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader, arguing the midterm results show voters want new leadership. Schumer says he has the votes to stay on; Democratic senators decide by secret ballot on Dec. 1.
stories.now: Van Hollen announced his bid on the MS NOW program hosted by Jen Psaki, calling himself the underdog but saying more than 10 senators back him. Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed endorsed him immediately, and Axios reports at least six incoming senators have said they will not support Schumer. Schumer, 75, responded that he has the votes to continue as Democratic leader. Common Dreams reported it would be the first contested race for the top Senate Democratic post in decades. Days earlier Van Hollen had said he had no plans to run.
stories.backstory: Schumer, of New York, has led Senate Democrats since 2017, as majority leader from 2021 to 2025 and minority leader since. Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the Nov. 3 midterms and take over in January. Schumer faced criticism within his party during the campaign, and Van Hollen broke with party leadership by endorsing El-Sayed in Michigan's Democratic primary in June. Whoever leads the majority decides which bills and nominees reach the Senate floor.

timeline.event: Van Hollen backs El-Sayed in Michigan, breaking with party leaders
Democrats win control of the Senate and House
Van Hollen announces challenge; Schumer says he has the votes
Senate Democrats scheduled to vote by secret ballot

stories.why: The majority leader controls the Senate's agenda, including whether and when votes on tariffs, spending and oversight of the White House happen. The contest is the first test of unity for Democrats since their midterm win.
stories.impact: There is no direct effect on Ontario for now. The winner will shape how hard the Senate pushes back on tariffs against Canada when the new Congress sits in January.

stories.headline: Nvidia slips again a day after Huang's exit as the search for a new CEO begins
stories.summary: Nvidia shares fell again in Friday morning trading, a day after co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive and the stock closed about 4% lower. Huang has agreed to answer U.S. lawmakers' questions behind closed doors by late November.
stories.now: Nvidia said Thursday that Huang resigned as president, chief executive and director, effective immediately. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is interim CEO while keeping her finance role, Harvey Jones becomes the company's first board chair, and the board says it will consider internal and external candidates for the permanent job. The shares fell about 13% at Thursday's open before closing roughly 4% lower; brokerage Schwab noted the stock is about 30% below its Oct. 6 peak of US$243.37. On Friday the stock rose early, then turned lower as the wider market fell, with the Nasdaq down about 1.6% by late morning. Brian Mast, the Republican who chairs the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said Huang has agreed to testify by U.S. Thanksgiving (Nov. 26) in a closed session; no date has been set. Members want to know whether a relationship with a woman U.S. officials reportedly believe worked for Chinese intelligence affected policy on exporting advanced chips; China has denied targeting Huang.
stories.backstory: Huang co-founded Nvidia and has run it since 1993, building it into the main supplier of the chips used to train artificial intelligence (AI) systems and one of the world's most valuable companies. Earlier this week, reports said the company had opened an internal investigation into whether he was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort through a relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who allegedly passed information to Beijing. Huang told staff in a company email that he had been unfaithful in his marriage. The stock had already slipped on that first report before Wednesday's news.

timeline.event: Board opens independent probe after report Huang was targeted by foreign intelligence
NYT reports second relationship; WSJ says board preparing to remove Huang
Board meets late in the day; shares fall after hours
Huang resigns; Kress named interim CEO; shares close down 4.3%

Shares slip again as wider U.S. market falls

stories.why: Nvidia is central to the artificial intelligence (AI) boom and one of the largest stocks in major U.S. indexes, and it has never had another chief executive. The spying allegation also raises national-security questions in Washington, which controls what chips the company may sell to China.
stories.impact: Most Canadian pension plans, index funds and RRSP or TFSA portfolios that track U.S. stocks hold Nvidia, so its swings show up in retirement savings here. The company's next results and its CEO search could bring more volatility.

stories.headline: Democrats hold Kansas governorship; Trump praises Mississippi winner Colom
stories.summary: The Associated Press on Thursday declared Democrat Cindy Holscher the winner of the Kansas governor's race, nine days after the vote, and Republican Ty Masterson conceded. President Trump praised Democrat Scott Colom, who won Mississippi's Senate seat a day earlier.
stories.now: Holscher, a state senator, beat Masterson, who had Trump's endorsement, in what local media call the closest Kansas governor's race in more than 50 years; station KSN reported her lead grew past 7,000 votes once late-arriving ballots were counted. The result keeps the governor's office in Democratic hands. Trump on Thursday praised Colom for campaigning among his supporters in the final days of the race. Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith conceded to Colom on Wednesday; he is the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi since 1982 and will be the state's first Black senator since the Reconstruction era after the Civil War. Mississippi counties must send official results to the secretary of state by Friday. Alaska is the last uncalled Senate race: Democrat Mary Peltola's lead over Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan narrowed to 3,975 first-choice votes after Wednesday's count, The Hill reported, with Peltola a little under 49% and Sullivan about 47%; the ranked-choice tabulation is set for Nov. 18.
stories.backstory: Republicans have held both chambers since January 2025, and all 435 House seats and about a third of the Senate were on the ballot. More than 53 million Americans voted early. Tariffs and high gas prices tied to the Iran war weighed on Trump's approval, and recent polls gave Democrats an edge in most key Senate races. Courts also turned back a Trump administration bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots.

timeline.event: Supreme Court rejects bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots
Cooper projected to flip North Carolina; Ossoff holds Georgia

stories.why: Colom's win in a state Republicans had held for more than four decades pads the Senate majority Democrats take over in January. A bigger majority makes it easier for them to block nominees, run investigations and force votes on tariffs.
stories.impact: Canadian exporters are watching whether a Democratic Congress moves to limit tariffs, which could ease pressure on Ontario manufacturers over time; near-term tariffs stay in place unless the White House changes them.

stories.headline: Ontario plans OSAP caps and online-program ban for private career colleges
stories.summary: Colleges Minister Nolan Quinn on Thursday outlined legislation that would limit how fast OSAP-funded enrolment can grow at private career colleges and cut off student aid for programs taught mainly online. The bill is expected to be tabled Monday.
stories.now: Quinn said the province found coordinated and sophisticated efforts to exploit the Ontario Student Assistance Program (OSAP), not just paperwork problems. The proposed law would cap growth in OSAP-funded enrolment at private institutions, make mostly-online programs ineligible, require career colleges to have a physical campus and restrict their ties to outside immigration and recruitment firms. It would also make private colleges liable for their students' loans, so the province can recover money more easily, and add new fines. The government has cited thousands of applications from the same internet address, final exams finished in about six minutes and outsiders doing students' coursework. Opposition parties dismissed it as a bill meant to protect the government that does nothing for students caught in the freeze on aid at career colleges, which began in early October and remains in place; the Liberals want funding restored at schools with no evidence of wrongdoing. Quinn has said the province is working with banks on low-interest loans for affected students until the pause is lifted in the new year.
stories.backstory: OSAP is Ontario's student loan and grant program. Online programs at private career colleges became eligible during the pandemic, and spending there grew quickly: seven career colleges accounted for about $385 million in grants in 2024-25, roughly as much as all of Ontario's public colleges combined. The province barred several schools over the summer, then paused OSAP payments to all private post-secondary institutions while the accounting firm KPMG audits the sector; early findings were sent to the Ontario Provincial Police and the auditor general. Separately, thousands of students walked out on Nov. 5 over wider OSAP and tuition changes.

stories.why: The province is trying to stop alleged large-scale misuse of public student aid without shutting out legitimate schools. How quickly it restarts payments decides whether thousands of students can continue their programs.
stories.impact: Students at private career colleges in the GTA still have no date for aid to resume, and those in mostly-online programs may lose eligibility altogether. Anyone enrolling should confirm a school's OSAP status before paying fees.

stories.headline: EU leaders in Dublin fail to settle who speaks for Europe in Ukraine talks
stories.summary: A day after Ukraine and U.S. envoys said Europe would join the next round of peace talks with Russia, European Union leaders meeting in Dublin on Friday had not agreed on who should represent them. Names in play include European Council President António Costa, foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas and Finland's President Alexander Stubb.
stories.now: Euronews and other outlets reported that leaders at Friday's informal summit debated whether a single envoy or a team should negotiate for Europe, without settling on a person or a mandate. Luxembourg's prime minister backed Costa, who said there was no division among leaders and that the right spokesperson depends on the subject. Kallas said that under EU rules the role falls to Costa, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and herself, and that agreeing on anything else would be hard. On Thursday, U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met President Vladimir Putin in Moscow and then briefed Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelenskyy near Dublin, where both sides said European partners would be included next time. Putin repeated Russia's opposition to foreign troops in Ukraine after any settlement, and the Abu Dhabi talks earlier in the week ended without agreement on territory or security guarantees.
stories.backstory: U.S.-mediated efforts to end the war stalled for months while Washington focused on Iran. Rubio said in May that the effort had stagnated. Europe has repeatedly asked to be included in any deal affecting its own security.

timeline.event: 314-prisoner swap; talks then stall

stories.why: A deal, or a breakdown, would shape European security and Canada's allied commitments. Disagreement between the U.S. and Europe is also a risk.
stories.impact: Peace progress could ease energy and grain prices over time. Canada, a NATO and G7 member, would feel the effects of any change in security arrangements.

stories.headline: Ousted Muskoka chair 'deeply disappointed' as backlash to Ford's regional picks grows
stories.summary: A day after Ontario named eight regional heads with 'strong chair' powers, Muskoka's replaced chair Jeff Lehman voiced his disappointment and Markham's mayor kept up criticism of Steven Del Duca's York appointment.
stories.now: Jeff Lehman, who was Muskoka's district chair until the province replaced him with Scott Aitchison, said Wednesday he was deeply disappointed by the decision. In York, Markham Mayor Frank Scarpitti called new chair Steven Del Duca, who stays on as Vaughan's mayor, deeply conflicted and no friend of Markham, and said the job gives one person overriding power over nine mayors and a roughly $5.2-billion regional budget. Del Duca said he will speak for all nine York municipalities and that none can be left behind. Municipal Affairs Minister Rob Flack rejected claims the picks are party insiders, noting Del Duca once led the Ontario Liberals; the other appointees are Kevin Ashe (Durham), Ann Mulvale (Halton), Frank Campion (Niagara), Nando Iannicca (Peel), Scott Davey (Waterloo) and Don McIsaac as Simcoe County warden. The chairs can hire or fire senior staff, veto some bylaws and propose the regional budget, and their term starts Nov. 15. Durham's new chair, Pickering Mayor Kevin Ashe, told CBC he is considering using the expanded powers on the regional budget, and Ontario New Democrat MPP Jeff Burch said the appointments undermine local democracy.
stories.backstory: Ontario first gave 'strong mayor' powers to Toronto and Ottawa in 2022 and later extended them to dozens of cities. This spring the province brought in the Better Regional Governance Act, letting it appoint chairs in Durham, Halton, Muskoka, Peel, Waterloo and York and the Simcoe warden, and cutting the size of Niagara's council. Some of these posts were previously chosen by voters or by regional councillors. The appointments come right after the Oct. 26 municipal elections.

stories.why: Regional governments run water, sewers, police budgets, roads and much of the planning that decides where housing goes. Appointed chairs with veto and staffing powers shift control toward Queen's Park.
stories.impact: For York, Peel, Durham and Halton residents, regional chairs now have more say over budgets that drive property taxes and over approvals for housing and infrastructure. Watch the first regional budgets under the new chairs.

stories.headline: Carney heads to Manila seeking trade deals with Southeast Asia
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney left Dublin for the Philippines, where he meets President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Saturday and hopes to conclude trade agreements with that country and with the wider Southeast Asian bloc. He goes on to Cambodia and then China, where he plans to raise foreign interference with President Xi Jinping.
stories.now: CBC reports Carney aims to finish two deals in Manila: one with the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and a separate one with the Philippines, which Ottawa projects could triple two-way trade by 2035. Canada also wants to sell more agri-food products, after obstacles for pork and pulses. The ASEAN summit opens Sunday, with Carney attending as a guest of the chair, and the Philippine Star reports President Trump is due to join on Nov. 17. In Dublin on Thursday, Carney was the only non-European leader at the European Political Community summit, said Canada has a role in security guarantees for Ukraine, and said closer European Union ties should bring more partnerships for Canada's auto sector. After Manila he attends the Francophonie summit in Phnom Penh and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders' meeting in Shenzhen on Nov. 18–19. At home, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre criticized the travel, saying the economy is about people struggling to make ends meet rather than summits.
stories.backstory: A federal public inquiry found that China was the most active foreign state trying to interfere in Canada's democratic institutions. Relations soured for years over arrests, tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles and Chinese duties on Canadian canola. Carney's government has since sought to rebuild trade ties with Beijing as tariffs from the Trump administration hit Canadian exports, which drew a tariff threat from Trump over any Canada-China deal.

timeline.event: Carney calls China Canada's top geopolitical threat

stories.why: The trip is part of Ottawa's effort to rely less on the United States for trade and defence. How Carney balances business with Beijing against security worries and pressure from Washington affects farmers, automakers and diaspora communities.
stories.impact: GTA residents with family or business ties to China are among those most exposed to interference concerns. Any trade easing could matter for Ontario exporters and for car buyers, while friction with the U.S. over China ties could complicate Canada-U.S. trade talks.

stories.headline: Canada's U.S. envoy warns tariffs are raising costs and chilling investment
stories.summary: Ambassador Mark Wiseman said tariff uncertainty is pushing up costs and discouraging business expansion, a day after Carney said the Trump administration remains Canada's main negotiating partner.
stories.now: Mark Wiseman, Canada's ambassador in Washington, told CNBC on Wednesday that uncertainty over tariffs is raising the cost of investing and putting companies off expanding, including in the United States. The federal government extended its tariff relief program beyond U.S. steel imports, so goods used by public education bodies, including those mandated by Indigenous organizations, can also qualify; Newsweek reports the program now runs to June 30, 2028, while exemptions are being withdrawn for some U.S. goods where Canadian alternatives exist. On Tuesday, Carney said the Trump administration remains the main authority on trade agreements even after Democrats won Congress, and Ottawa will keep working toward a deal that suits Canada. Democrats have pledged to try to repeal tariffs on Canada, but they would need Republican votes to override a veto. Trump has also threatened new tariffs on Canadian vehicles starting in January.
stories.backstory: Canada has used remission and relief measures to soften the cost of counter-tariffs on its own importers. A recent Finance Canada report found Ottawa approved about $5.6 billion in relief against a projected $2.2 billion, with more than 800 requests still unresolved.

stories.impact: Schools and some public bodies in Ontario may face lower costs on imported goods. Businesses importing affected goods may be able to apply for relief.

stories.headline: Immigration minister hits back after Poilievre calls budget plan 'bonkers'
stories.summary: Immigration Minister Lena Diab on Thursday defended the immigration measures in last week's federal budget as temporary and aimed at people already in Canada, after Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre attacked the plan in a video.
stories.now: In a video released Sunday, Poilievre called the plan 'bonkers' and claimed it would admit about 200,000 more permanent residents a year than under former prime minister Justin Trudeau, arguing that population growth has outpaced housing, health care and jobs. Diab said Thursday that the measure is targeted and time-limited, meant to help provinces fill labour needs with workers who already live in Canada and to clear a badly backlogged humanitarian stream, and that it is not a lasting rise in immigration levels. She said she does not think Poilievre understands Canada. Prime Minister Carney has called the levels plan sustainable. The exchange comes ahead of six federal byelections on Dec. 7, including a close race in Brantford–Brant South.
stories.backstory: Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne tabled the Carney government's second budget on Nov. 5, projecting a $62.3-billion deficit for 2026-27 and about $142 billion in new spending over five years. The immigration levels plan, which sets how many permanent residents Canada aims to admit, was released with it. Ottawa cut its targets in 2024 and 2025 after rapid population growth put pressure on housing and services. Permanent residents can live and work in Canada indefinitely and later apply for citizenship.

timeline.event: Ottawa cuts permanent-resident targets

stories.why: Immigration levels shape population growth, the labour supply and housing demand. The dispute is also an early test of each party's message before byelections that could change the Liberals' slim majority.
stories.impact: The GTA receives a large share of Canada's newcomers, so the targets affect rents, hiring and demand for services here. People already working in Ontario on temporary permits may find a clearer route to permanent status.

stories.headline: Teen gets two years in custody for shootings at Vaughan and Toronto synagogues
stories.summary: A youth who was 17 when shots were fired at two Toronto-area synagogues in March has been sentenced to two years in custody followed by a year of supervision in the community, police said Thursday. Jewish groups say whoever paid for and organized the attacks has still not been identified.
stories.now: The youth, identified only as J.B. because of his age, pleaded guilty to firearms offences and was sentenced Tuesday in Newmarket by Ontario Court Justice Michael Townsend, who accepted a joint recommendation from the Crown and the defence. Several outlets describe the three-year term as the maximum available for these offences under the Youth Criminal Justice Act. The shots hit Beth Avraham Yoseph of Toronto, a synagogue in Vaughan, and Shaarei Shomayim in Toronto; no one was hurt, but both buildings were damaged. The Friends of Simon Wiesenthal Center said court records show the teen was paid to carry out the shootings. No hate-related charges were part of this case, and an 18-year-old was also charged in May.
stories.backstory: The two synagogues were hit by gunfire on the same night in March, part of a series of attacks on Jewish institutions in the GTA since 2023 that has included repeated shootings at a girls' school in North York. York Regional Police and Toronto police investigated together. Police charged an 18-year-old on May 6 and arrested a 17-year-old later that month. Canadian law bars publishing the names of accused who are under 18.

timeline.event: Shots fired at synagogues in Vaughan and Toronto; no injuries

stories.why: The case is one of the few to reach sentencing after a run of attacks on Jewish sites in the GTA. The finding that the shooter was paid leaves open who ordered the attacks and why.
stories.impact: Synagogues and Jewish schools in York Region and Toronto continue to operate with extra security and police patrols. Community groups are pressing police to find those who directed the shootings.
